takeaways: Saint Paul is quieter than Minneapolis at night. There are good spots along West 7th and downtown, but for lots of late-night options you'll often cross the river.
Its historic architecture is unmatched: Summit Avenue runs 4.5 miles from the Cathedral to the Mississippi, and Summit Hill, Cathedral Hill and Macalester-Groveland share that older, tree-lined feel.
The flip side: little new construction. If a brand-new home is a must, Saint Paul has few options.
Outdoors: Como Park Zoo and Conservatory is free every day, Harriet Island sits on the river, and the city has more than 200 miles of bike paths and lanes.
Potholes and road construction are a real part of life, with the freeze-thaw cycle and many MnDOT projects running through the city.
You'll likely need a car, though transit is improving: the Gold Line (2025) to Woodbury, the B and E lines, and the Green Line Extension (2027).

Strengths include a food scene with James Beard recognition, the Hmong Village and Hmongtown markets, the Science Museum, the Winter Carnival and the State Fair, plus colleges such as Macalester, St. Thomas, Hamline and St. Catherine. Shopping is the weak spot: Grand Avenue is charming but small.

faq.q: Is Saint Paul quieter than Minneapolis?
faq.a: Yes. Saint Paul has a slower, more residential feel, with good bars and music venues but fewer late-night options than Minneapolis.

faq.q: Is there new construction in Saint Paul?
faq.a: Not much. The city's historic, built-out neighborhoods leave little room for new homes, so buyers who want new construction usually look to the suburbs.

takeaways: There's no single best place to live in Minnesota, only the best place for your commute, budget and weekly routine.

Minneapolis: real city life with parks near almost every home and distinct neighborhoods (North Loop, Northeast, Lowry Hill East). Trade-offs: smaller yards, higher city property taxes, and most people still need a car.
Saint Paul: older homes and a slower pace (Highland Park, Summit Hill, Macalester-Groveland). Fewer late-night options, and a long drive if your job is to the west.
Plymouth: a practical west-metro pick with parks, lakes and easy access to Minneapolis and western job centers. Not very walkable, and prices can surprise you.
Eden Prairie: planned and convenient, near the airport, with the Green Line Extension (16 stations, expected 2027) ending there. Still car-dependent and pricey.
Edina: close-in, established neighborhoods and 50th and France. Run the real monthly numbers, including property taxes, before you fall for a street.
Maple Grove (about 3,600 new housing units since 2020) and Woodbury (more than 4,200) offer newer homes, but each works best if your life stays on its side of the metro.

Lakeville added about 4,900 housing units from 2020 to 2025, the most in Minnesota, and paused new residential plat applications for up to a year in 2026, though already-approved lots can still be built. Rochester, home to Mayo Clinic, is its own decision, about 90 minutes from the metro.

faq.q: Is Lakeville still building new homes?
faq.a: Yes. In 2026 Lakeville paused new residential plat applications for up to a year, but already-approved projects, including about 675 single-family lots and 644 townhome units, can still be built, according to the video.

faq.q: What is the best suburb of Minneapolis?
faq.a: It depends on where you work and how you live. Jason's rule: pick by your commute, your budget and your Saturday routine, and drive the neighborhoods before deciding.

takeaways: Jason sorts 10 suburbs into tiers by price and what you trade for it. The lower tiers aren't worse places; they give you more for less money with a longer drive.
Lakeville: median about $477,000, along I-35 about 20 to 25 minutes from the airport and 25 to 35 from either downtown, with more than 70 parks and nearly 150 miles of trails.
Prior Lake: median about $490,000, with about 15 lakes in and around the city and roughly 1,000 acres of parkland. It's lake living at a lower price than the west metro.
Stillwater (median about $475,000) and Excelsior (median about $890,000 on Lake Minnetonka) sell historic charm and water over convenience.
Eden Prairie (median about $598,000) and Chanhassen (about $575,000): parks, trails and highway access without top-tier prices.

Plymouth (median about $525,000, homes selling in about 21 days) and Minnetonka: established neighborhoods, larger lots and mature trees. Expect fast competition, and older homes in Minnetonka may need updates.
Wayzata (median listing price around $2.3 million) and Edina (median about $760,000) are the top tier, where you pay for the address, lake access and walkable districts like 50th and France.
These prices are as stated in the video (December 2025); check our market reports for current numbers.

faq.q: What are the most expensive suburbs of Minneapolis?
faq.a: Wayzata and Edina top Jason's list: Wayzata's median listing price was around $2.3 million and Edina's median sale price around $760,000 at the time of the video.

faq.q: What are affordable suburbs with lakes near Minneapolis?
faq.a: Prior Lake and Lakeville in the south metro offer lake living and newer homes for less than the west-metro lake suburbs, with a longer drive to downtown.

takeaways: This 2022 video covers ten reasons to live in the Minneapolis area. Lakes come first: Minnesota has thousands, which means cabins, lake homes and fishing within reach.
The Mall of America in Bloomington has about 5.6 million square feet and more than 500 stores.
Long summer evenings: in June and July it can stay light until about 10 p.m.
Every major pro sport plays here (the Vikings, Twins, Timberwolves, Wild, Lynx and Minnesota United), plus college sports.
The music scene includes First Avenue and the legacy of Prince and Bob Dylan, and there are more than 80 craft breweries in the Twin Cities.
Outdoors: parks, rail-to-trail paths, boating, biking, skiing and the North Shore near Duluth.
The State Fair ("the Great Minnesota Get-Together") draws close to 2 million people over 12 days, and housing costs far less than on the coasts, with one of the nation's highest homeownership rates.

faq.q: How big is the Mall of America?
faq.a: About 5.6 million square feet with more than 500 stores, in Bloomington, according to the video.

faq.q: How many people go to the Minnesota State Fair?
faq.a: Close to 2 million over its 12 days in late August, according to the video.

takeaways: A tour of a large vacation rental in Spooner, Wisconsin, on its own island reached by a bridge, with about 1,000 feet of lakeshore.
The main house is about 13,000 square feet with 21 bedrooms, about 10 living areas, multiple kitchens, a home theater, a game room and four sets of washers and dryers, and it sleeps about 80 people.
Two separate cottages, a pool, two hot tubs, a pizza oven, pickleball courts and disc golf round out the property.
What makes a vacation rental work, in Jason's view: memorable, unique spaces that make guests want to come back.

takeaways: Fieldstone and rubble foundations, common in homes built before about 1920 in neighborhoods like Seward, Longfellow, Summit Hill, Powderhorn and parts of Northeast, can shift with each freeze-thaw cycle. Watch for bowed walls, loose stones, moisture and cracks wider than a quarter inch, and get a structural engineer's report.
Freshly painted basement walls can hide efflorescence and cracks. Major foundation repairs can run $20,000 to $60,000, according to Jason.

Old boilers and radiators (common in homes from 1900 to 1940): replacement can cost $10,000 to $20,000 or more, and adding air conditioning without ductwork often means mini-splits. Hire a boiler specialist, not just a general inspector.
Grading and drainage: soil should slope at least 6 inches away from the house in the first 10 feet, and downspouts should carry water 10 to 15 feet away.
Knob-and-tube wiring (common before about 1930) can make a home hard to insure. A full rewire can run $15,000 to $25,000 or more; get a licensed electrician's inspection and proof of permits.
Roofs: older and flat roofs are vulnerable to snow load and ice dams. Check attic insulation (Minnesota code calls for R-49) and ventilation, and be wary of judging a roof under snow.
Basements: Minnesota ranks among the top states for radon. Testing is inexpensive, mitigation usually runs about $1,700 to $5,000, and a drain tile system with a sealed sump is a green flag.
Updated pre-1940 homes with documented system upgrades sell fastest, while those with unresolved foundation, wiring or boiler issues sit longer and sell at a discount.

faq.q: What is knob-and-tube wiring and why does it matter?
faq.a: An early, ungrounded wiring system found in many homes built before about 1930. Many insurers limit or deny coverage on homes that still have it, and a full rewire often costs $15,000 to $25,000 or more.

faq.q: Should I worry about a fieldstone foundation?
faq.a: Not automatically, but get a structural engineer's report. Fieldstone foundations can shift with freeze-thaw cycles; watch for bowed walls, loose stones, moisture and wide cracks.
